opening.headline: To prevent dissatisfaction from pouring in after distributing the product only with the feeling that “it seems to be working well,” a set of representative questions divided into core, exception, and boundary and criteria for correct answers are needed.
body: After using it a few times, it seemed to work well, so I distributed the assistant to my team, but after a week, it is common for complaints to pile up saying, “It gives the wrong time period,” and “The answer is different every time.” This is because feelings are evaluations that change depending on what questions I ask.

In this class, we will look at how to create a representative set of questions by dividing the questions the assistant will receive into core, exception, and boundary, and how to write down the expected response criteria for each question in advance. Next, you will learn reproducible confirmation by checking again before and after modification with the same set, and explain the return information assistant's question set as an example.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain what a representative set of questions and criteria for correct answers are
Can distinguish between core questions, exception questions, and boundary questions

screens.title: I distributed it with the feeling that “it seems to be going well.”
screens.lead: First, read the story of the team that deployed the Returns Assistant.

visual.alt: A picture showing in chronological order the scene of distribution after being used a few times and the scene of dissatisfaction accumulating a week later.
labels: It seems to be going well
The answer is different every time

paragraphs: One team created a return information assistant and used it a few times. After asking a few questions, the answers seemed plausible, so I distributed them to the entire team, saying, "It seems to be working well."

After a week, complaints began to build. The content was, “The return period is incorrectly provided,” and “The answer to the same question is different every time.” Most of the questions asked before deployment were easy ones, and the questions that raised complaints were ones that had never been checked.

Feeling is an evaluation that changes depending on what questions I ask. On the other hand, if you have a set of questions, you can check them again using the same criteria no matter who checks them and when. This lesson covers how to create that set of questions.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If all the questions asked before deployment were easy questions, what was the basis for judging that it was ‘going well’?

screens.outro: First, let me recall what questions I asked before deployment.

screens.title: What questions did you ask before deploying your new assistant?
screens.lead: If you first think about each question in your head and then select it, the instructor will organize your thoughts. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Can you name three questions you get asked most often?
items.answer: The most frequently asked question is closest to the reason the assistant exists. If you find it difficult to name these three, it may mean that your assistant's purpose is not yet clear. These questions become the center of the question set.

items.prompt: Have you ever asked a question that was intentionally difficult?
items.answer: Questions with exceptions or questions that span the baseline can be intentionally created and checked. In fact, users become frustrated when they ask these questions. In this class, we will address these questions by dividing them into exceptions and boundaries.

screens.outro: Let us now look at the composition of a representative set of questions.

screens.title: Representative set of questions: core, exceptions, boundaries
screens.lead: Select the arrows to go through each of the three types of questions that make up the question set. At the end, see where you repeat this set of questions.

visual.alt: Percentage plot showing a set of 20 questions divided into three chunks: core, exceptions, and boundaries.
labels: Exception question (when exception conditions are attached)

steps.title: What is a question set?
steps.body: A representative question set is a list of questions that your assistant will be asked. Rather than collecting random questions, organize them in a balanced manner by dividing them into core, exceptions, and boundaries. This will help you avoid the illusion of passing only easy questions.

steps.title: key questions
steps.body: This is the most frequently asked question and features the most in the set. In terms of return information, 'Can I simply change my mind and return the product?', 'How many days is the return period?' Same question. If you make a mistake here, most users will be affected, so check this first.

steps.title: exception question
steps.body: Ask about cases where there are exceptions to the rule. This is a case where a conclusion is different from the general rule, such as ‘Can sale items be returned?’ or ‘What happens to opened products?’ It catches problems where your assistant misses exceptions and only speaks general rules.

steps.title: boundary question
steps.body: This is a question that is so close to the baseline that the conclusion can be different with just one step. An example is ‘Can I apply on the last day of the regulation after receipt?’ This is also the most common area of ​​frustration, as it reveals how the assistant reads the baseline.

steps.title: Where to use question sets
steps.body: After creating a Gem or GPT, it provides a flow to check the response and modify the instructions by adding a prompt in Preview. A set of questions becomes a list of inputs in this Preview that repeat the same sentences over and over again. GPT instructs you to check whether the knowledge file is used as intended even after uploading it in Preview.

screens.outro: If you have a question, the next step is to decide what you consider to be the correct response.

screens.title: Correct answer criteria: Write down in advance what will be considered a correct response
screens.lead: The table below is an example of the expected response criteria for each question from the return assistant. For each question, read what facts should and should not be included. The return period in the example is for illustrative purposes only.

data.caption: Example of return assistant response expectations (assuming return period is 7 days from receipt)
columns: Contents that should not be entered
rows: How many days is the return period?
Period within 7 days of receipt and how to apply
State the period first in one sentence and then explain how to apply.
Separate conditions applicable to sale items
Answer that applies the general product rules as is
Can I apply on the 7th day after receiving it?
Judgment of possibility and basis provisions, including base date
Place the conclusion first, then the evidence
Return availability and conditions for opened products
Organizing conditions and processing in table format
data.notes: The standards must be written in detail and in a format so that people can read them and make the same decision. Words like ‘natural’ and ‘kind’ alone can make a difference.

screens.outro: Once you have written down the criteria, we will outline how to determine whether the response met the criteria.

screens.title: Boundary cases and reproducible confirmation
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare the implications for handling edge cases and reproducible verification.

states.label: borderline case
states.body: A borderline case is a question where the conclusion is different by one step. Placing the questions you ask on the 6th, 7th, and 8th day after receipt side by side will reveal where your assistant draws the line. When creating boundary questions, structure them differently and in a form that actual users would likely ask. The examples in the prompt document also resemble actual uses and guide you to configure them differently.

states.label: Reproducible confirmation
states.body: Reproducible verification means that everyone uses the same questions and the same criteria. The question sets are rerun in the same order before and after modification, and compared by marking whether or not the criteria were met in the same way. Then, rather than saying, “I think it’s improved,” you can say things like, “9 out of 10 key questions meet the criteria.” It has value as confirmation only if the same results are obtained no matter who checks and when.

screens.outro: Now let’s apply it directly to the return information assistant.

screens.title: Explanation: Returns Assistant's Question Set
screens.lead: The instructor will narrate the process of creating a set of questions for the Return Assistant to begin with. Select the arrow to move on.

steps.title: Gather key questions
steps.body: We've collected the most frequently asked questions. ‘Is it possible to return a product simply because I changed my mind?’, ‘How many days does it take?’ The same questions are taken from actual inquiry records. Organize around ten or so to make up the largest portion of the set.

steps.title: Add exception question
steps.body: Ask questions about cases where return conditions change, such as for sale items or opened items. If you look for clauses in the regulatory documents that are written ‘but only if,’ they will provide you with material for asking exception questions.

steps.title: Add boundary question
steps.body: Create questions that span the baseline, such as if you are applying on the last day of the post-receipt rule. If you put the last day, one day before, and one day back side by side, you can see at a glance how to read the baseline.

steps.title: Write down expected response criteria
steps.body: Write down that each question must include the period and application method of the regulatory document, and that arbitrary dates should not be created. Format standards are also listed. It's like saying the conclusion first and then putting the evidence behind it.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: This set of about 20 pieces made this way is the ruler of this assistant. The method of judging by feeling after using it a few times has changed to the method of checking again at any time using the same questions and the same standards.

screens.outro: After spinning the set, you need to read the results and determine the next correction point.

screens.title: Commentary: Read the results and decide the next correction point
screens.lead: As you select each step, the instructor's commentary unfolds. Give the question set a spin and see how you read the results.

items.answer: Each question is marked as met, partially met, or not met based on the expected response criteria. Using the same display method makes it easy to compare before and after modifications.
If key questions are found to be unmet, they will be addressed as a top priority. Because it affects the most users. Questions of exceptions and boundaries come next.

items.prompt: 3. What to do if you only waver on boundary questions
items.answer: If you get the core questions right but only falter on the boundary questions, it may be a sign that your guidelines lack rules for reading the baseline. Reinforce rules such as whether or not to include reference dates in guidelines.

items.prompt: 4. What do you do after editing?
items.answer: After making corrections, repeat the same set of questions to check. Not only do we see whether the areas we fixed have improved, but we also see whether other questions have become worse.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: A set of questions is the ruler of quality
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.

paragraphs: The quality of the assistant is checked not by feeling, but by questions and standards set. The question set should include key points, exceptions, and boundaries to avoid the illusion of passing only easy questions.

For each question, write down the expected response criteria in facts and form in advance, and then go through the same set again in the same order before and after revision. This way, you can catch problems before deployment that you might only find out about after complaints start pouring in. The set of questions is not something you create once and be done with; it is a list that you expand upon as new complaints come in.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Put key, exception, and boundary questions together, write down your criteria in advance, and check them again with the same set.

checks.q: In the Returns Assistant's question set, what type of question is 'Can I apply on the last day of the policy after receipt?'
checks.explain: Questions where the outcome changes by a single step closer to the baseline, such as on the last day of a deadline, are boundary questions.

wrong.0: Key questions are the most frequently asked general questions.
wrong.1: Exception questions ask about cases where there are exception conditions, such as sale items or opened products.
wrong.3: A type of question is not a set of questions; the format is part of the expected response criteria.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Put them in the right order to improve your assistant with a set of questions
items: Write down the expected response criteria for each question in advance.
Return responses to the same set of questions to indicate whether the criteria are met
Addressing unmet key questions as a top priority
After editing, check again with the same set of questions.
checks.explain: To compare changes, you must first set the standards, judge them, revise them in order of priority, and then check them again with the same set.
checks.intro: Put them in order, remembering the order you learned them. Results are not recorded.

glossary.def: This is a representative list of questions your assistant will be asked, with highlights, exceptions, and boundaries.
This is a judgment standard that pre-writes the facts and format that must be included in the response to each question.
These are questions near the baseline where small differences in the conclusions can make a difference.
This is a method of comparing before and after modification again using the same questions and the same criteria.

misconceptions.myth: You can tell the quality after using it a few times.
misconceptions.fact: The impression varies depending on the question asked. A set of questions must be determined so that no matter who checks them, the same judgment can be reached.

misconceptions.myth: A lot of easy questions are enough.
misconceptions.fact: The real complaints usually come from exceptions and boundary questions. You won't find these problems by just passing easy questions.

misconceptions.myth: You can tell the criteria for correct answers by looking at them.
misconceptions.fact: Judgments vary from person to person. You must specifically write down the facts that should be included, the content that should not be included, and the format.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The set of questions is the gauge of quality.
Put key, exception, and boundary questions together.
Write down the expected response criteria in facts and form in advance.
Check again before and after correction with the same set.

closing.reflection: What are the top five questions my assistant will ask?
